- A self-reported sleep item also scored in a mapped scale fills the self row ('also scored in \<row>'), but a parent's item scored in a mapped scale never fills the parent row, and a proxy or donor-imputed answer is NA on the self row.

### Body size, activity and early life

- `hlth_bmi` takes kg/m2 at the occasion, measured or reported, as released or computed from height and weight.
- Where one occasion has more than one BMI source, take measured, then the child's own report, then a parent's report, and name the others as unused.
- `hlth_bmi_measure` records whether height and weight were measured, self-reported or parent-reported, filled per row where the source differs within a wave, an exception to the `*_measure` rules: compatible where a source column records the source, and 'Unknown' only when a value exists but its source cannot be identified.
- A released BMI-for-age z-score goes to `hlth_bmi_z`, with its growth reference in `hlth_bmi_z_measure`, only where neither BMI nor the height and weight to compute it are released; otherwise z-scores are derived at analysis on one reference, and percentile-only and category-only releases are incompatible.
- Height, weight, BMI and birth-weight values are kept as entered, including entries only possible in another unit, and are screened at analysis, as screen time and sleep are.
- `hlth_pa_days60` takes only the days-of-60-minutes item, past 7 days or a usual week (the past 7 days where both are asked, never their mean); day bands take their midpoint (partial), and every other activity format is incompatible.
- BMI, BMI z-scores and activity days are never carried across waves.
- `hlth_puberty_status` takes a published pubertal-status measure as the instrument scores it (Pubertal Development Scale mean or category score, Tanner stage), higher = more advanced, from any informant (examiner, then the child, then a parent where an occasion has more than one), described in `hlth_puberty_measure` and standardised within dataset, sex and measure at analysis; an onset or menarche item alone is proximate.
- `hlth_maturity_offset` takes years from predicted peak height velocity from a named anthropometric equation (Mirwald or Moore), released or computed from the occasion's measures; neither pubertal row is ever carried across waves.
- The early-life rows describe the child's birth and infancy and are carried by the carry-forward rule.
- Birth weight is in grams: closed bands at their midpoint, an open band half the neighbouring band's width beyond its bound (partial); low-birth-weight flags are incompatible.
- Preterm means before 37 completed weeks; a yes/no item with another cut or none, including 'born 3 weeks or more early', is partial.
- Breastfeeding is ever or never: any duration above zero is TRUE.
- Smoking in pregnancy is TRUE for any smoking at any point in the pregnancy; the mother's smoking at another time and household smoking are incompatible.

### SES

- **Household SES cuts:** Low, Medium and High split the unweighted sample 40/20/40 within wave, and within country or site where the measure or its bands are country- or site-specific; at or below the 40th percentile is Low and above the 60th is High.
- A banded or discrete source classifies each band by its ridit in the same frame (below 0.4 Low, 0.4 to 0.6 Medium, above 0.6 High); if no band falls in 0.4 to 0.6, the band nearest 0.5 is Medium.
- A fixed class scheme keeps its standard three-way collapse (proximate), and subjective standing is cut at its labelled anchors with the midpoint as Medium.
- Income, income-to-needs, affluence or a composite index is compatible when every level lies within 10 points of 40/20/40 in every wave, and proximate otherwise.
- Multi-country repeated cross-sections cut within country and cycle.
- Area SES uses the index's own national quintiles, never sample quantiles.
- School-level indicators (school type, fees, funding, track) map to neither SES row; mark them incompatible with a one-line note, put a public/private sector item on `school_sector` and a track or programme item on `school_track`.
- `ses_household_measure` reads '\<type>: \<measure>', with the type from a fixed list.
- Parent education uses one vocabulary with ISCED anchors; a band spanning two levels goes to the level holding most of its members (proximate), and tertiary study begun but not completed is Post-secondary.
- Parents are whichever mother and father figures the source records, with the row partial when one is systematically unobserved.
- `maternal_employment` takes the mother figure's paid work now or in the past week (Employed or Not employed); a longer window or an occupation list with a homemaker option is proximate, and the occupation of a current or most recent job is not employment status (incompatible).
- Categorical SES rows are compatible when every level matches the schema's meaning and proximate for coarser, lumped or stand-in sources (school location, subjective standing, occupational class); they never use partial, and constants are inferred.
- Urbanicity follows a national typology on its own thresholds; raw size bands use under 5,000 Rural, 5,000 to under 100,000 Suburban and 100,000 or more Urban.
- An urban constant is allowed only when the design guarantees urban residence at the measured wave.

## Keeping variables.csv in sync with the dataschema

When the dataschema gains a variable, every dataset's `variables.csv` needs a matching row.
Don't do this by hand:

```r
targets::tar_source()
sync_harmonisation_vars() # all datasets, plus the new-dataset template
```

This appends any missing variables as `in_progress` and reorders rows to dataschema order, keeping any measure-tagged rows after the primary rows.
It covers the template under `harmonisation/templates/dataset/` as well, so a newly copied dataset spec starts with the full set of variables.
The validator (and therefore CI) rejects a `variables.csv` with missing, duplicate, or unknown target variables.

## Checking your expressions

Before running the pipeline or the test suite, you can check every `expression` in one go:

```r
targets::tar_source()
check_harmonisation_exprs()
```

It returns one row per problem — an empty tibble means everything is fine — with the columns `variables_file`, `target_variable`, `measure`, `status`, `issue`, `message`, `suggestion`, and `fixed`.
There are four kinds of `issue`:

| Issue | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `parse_error` | The expression is not valid R and will fail the moment it is evaluated. |
| `unknown_function` | It calls a function that is neither base R, allowlisted, nor namespaced (see [Writing expressions](#writing-expressions)). |
| `missing_expression` | The status says the row is evaluated, but no expression was given. |
| `unformatted` | It is valid, but [Air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air) would format it differently; `suggestion` holds the reformatted text. |

The first three are what CI enforces, so a clean run here means the expressions will survive the test suite.
Formatting is advisory only and is never enforced by CI — pass `check_format = FALSE` to skip it, which also avoids needing Air installed.
Air ships inside a VS Code extension in this devcontainer, and that directory is only on the *terminal's* `PATH`, so `Sys.which("air")` comes up empty in an R console; the check looks in the extension directory too, and warns rather than failing if it finds nothing.

By default only rows with an evaluated status are checked, matching what the harmoniser actually runs.
Pass `active_only = FALSE` to include `in_progress` and other skipped rows while you are still drafting them.

### Fixing formatting

`fix = TRUE` writes each `suggestion` back into the `expression` column and reports what it changed in the `fixed` column:

```r
check_harmonisation_exprs(fix = TRUE)
```

Only `unformatted` rows are rewritten; the other three issues need a human decision and are left untouched.
Every other column is read and written as text, so a fix cannot disturb cells it was not asked to change.

Expressions are formatted to their own settings rather than the ones in the repository's `air.toml`, which continues to govern the `.R` files:

| Setting | Default | Why |
|---------|---------|-----|
| `line_width` | `120` | An expression in a CSV cell has no surrounding indentation to pay for, and the 80-column default explodes ordinary recodes into one argument per line. |
| `persistent_line_breaks` | `FALSE` | Air normally keeps a call expanded if the source has a line break straight after the opening `(`. In a CSV cell that break reflects hand-editing rather than intent, so width alone should decide. |

Both are arguments, so you can widen or narrow a run without editing any configuration.

## Testing your harmonisation

```r
targets::tar_make(names = harmonised_BPIPD_9999) # your dataset id
targets::tar_read(harmonised_BPIPD_9999)
```

Check derived values look sensible (tabulate `sex`, summarise `age_years`, …).
Then run the repository test suite, which validates all harmonisation metadata without needing the data:

```r
testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")
```

Both run on every pull request — CI validates the metadata and expressions, but only your local `tar_make()` sees real values.

## The combined analysis table

`targets::tar_make()` row-binds every harmonised dataset into one table, `analysis_data`.
Before it is stored, each character column with at most 1,000 distinct non-missing values is converted to a factor, so the table loads quickly ([DR-0006](../decisions/DR-0006-analysis-data-storage.md)).
Columns with more distinct values, such as `participant_id`, `survey_cluster` and `survey_strata`, stay character.
The levels are the values that occur in the data, in byte order (upper case before lower case); `allowed_values` in the dataschema is not used.
A subset keeps every level of the full table, so use `droplevels()` when empty levels get in the way, and `as.numeric(as.character(x))` rather than `as.numeric(x)` to turn a factor of numbers back into numbers.

`analysis_data` is stored as a Parquet file.
`targets::tar_read(analysis_data)` returns within seconds because `arrow` converts each column to an ordinary R vector only when it is first used.
Select the columns you need before filtering or mutating: an operation that touches every column of the lazily loaded table, such as `dplyr::filter()` on the full table, is about three times slower than on ordinary vectors.
For whole-table work, setting `options(arrow.use_altrep = FALSE)` before reading converts every column up front, which makes later operations fast but briefly needs about twice the table's memory.
`arrow` can also read only some columns, or filter and summarise before anything is loaded:

```r
path <- targets::tar_path_target(analysis_data)

# Only the columns you need
arrow::read_parquet(path, col_select = c(dataset_id, wave, sex, age_years))

# A lazy query: nothing is loaded until collect()
arrow::open_dataset(path) |>
  dplyr::filter(st_measure_id == "primary") |>
  dplyr::count(dataset_id, sex) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```
